utterances.text: You reported in February of 1992 and were assigned to work at the TO in Novi Travnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was that at the municipal secretariat of the TO in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: No. The building was the same building where the MUP was housed and the TO staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you arrived in February of 1992, what position did you take and what were your specific duties?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: It wasn't any particular position. We all worked doing everything involved in the formation of units. I didn't have any specific assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How long did you work without a specific assignment?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: All the time while I was working in the TO staff, there were no specific assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What I'm trying to get at, and perhaps you can assist me, Brigadier, what specifically did you do there?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Specifically, probably because I came as a career military man, I trained men in the use of mortars, of 60 and 82 millimetre calibre, in the village of Vezovici and Sakovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was that your principal function between February of 1992, until the date when you left the Territorial Defence in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I take it you have some degree of speciality, Brigadier, in respect to artillery pieces if you were engaged in the training of individuals with mortars; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Not a certain degree, but due to the work I did before, I had to be familiar with everything, including artillery pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Other than the training of the soldiers that you've just described, did you do anything else in terms of intelligence gathering, or did you do anything in respect of intelligence gathering while you were working at the TO?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you collect any documents from the TO while you were working at the TO in February of 1992 until the time when you left the TO?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you collect any documents from the TO and take them with you when you left in March of 1992 and went to the municipal headquarters of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: I didn't need to do that because I was familiar with them. I didn't take any documents at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you prepare any notebooks in respect of information that you had seen at the Territorial Defence in Novi Travnik while you were there?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, what specific date, Brigadier, did you leave the Territorial Defence and transfer to the municipal headquarters of the HVO in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why did you transfer from the Territorial Defence to the municipal headquarters of the HVO in March of 1993 -- I'm sorry, March of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Because the municipal TO staff had simply become one single ethnic, and they were appointing people for commanders and chiefs of staff, and my name did not figure anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you say that the Territorial Defence became monoethnic in Novi Travnik in February to March of 1992. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: I didn't say February/March. I said from the time I left, no one else was left there, except I can't recall whether there were any Serbs, but in any case, there were no Croats left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While you were at the TO, did you work with an individual by the name of Ivica Kobanac?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: No. I don't know anyone by that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you transferred to the municipal headquarters of the HVO in Novi Travnik sometime in March. Could you tell us, please, what your duties and responsibilities were at the municipal headquarters of the HVO in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: At first, I had operative tasks, that is, drawing up lists of units and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Lists of HVO units?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I understood your answer, you said when you first got to the HVO municipal headquarters in Novi Travnik, you drew up lists of units, and that sort of thing. That's what the answer shows on the monitor. My question is: Were those lists of units that you drew up lists of HVO units?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I mostly participated in organising the HVO headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So you did not draw up lists of Territorial Defence units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: I didn't need to do that because I knew them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in participating in the organisation of the HVO headquarters, did you have any other duties and responsibilities while you were at the TO headquarters -- I'm sorry, at the HVO municipal headquarters in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Later, I was deputy chief of staff of the HVO of Novi Travnik, and when the commander of the municipal headquarters, Ljubas, was arrested by the army of the Bosnian Serbs, I became the commander for a short time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When did you become the assistant chief of staff of HVO headquarters intelligence affairs?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Roughly in July 1992, July or August. I do not recall the exact date, but it was at the beginning of the formation of the command for the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What were your principal tasks in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: My principal tasks were to collect and process data about the army of Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you also collect and process information about the Territorial Defence and the Armija?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When did you start collecting the information about the Armija and the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: When the first open attack began against the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: That was on the 20th to the 21st of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before that, Brigadier, neither you nor your colleagues collected information about the ABiH or the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you about some of the testimony that you gave us last week, and that is, when you described the job that you had, you indicated that you collected intelligence through three means. As I recall your testimony, Brigadier, teamwork, reconnaissance and observation. Those are the three means and methods of collecting intelligence data that you described. My first question is: What did you mean by "teamwork"? Did you be more explicit?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Perhaps the interpretation was not quite good, when I used "teamwork," I meant the work of all of us, and in that joint effort, we all worked together. We all had a common enemy, that is, the Bosnian Serb army, and we were familiar with the units and the deployment of the BH army, as they knew our own forces and deployment of the HVO. This went on until the first open conflict erupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So in the course of collecting and compiling information about the Bosnian Serb units along the confrontation lines, I take it part of your job and responsibility was to plot, either on a map or in some way of recording, the locations of the opposition units that confronted the HVO and the Territorial Defence forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you do that with a map, and would you have locations of particular units plotted on maps?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: What units are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm referring, Brigadier, to the enemy units. So along the Serbian lines, would you plot the locations of which brigades and which units were at which locations along the Serb/HVO/Territorial Defence confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At the same time, Brigadier, would you also be aware of where your own units were along that same confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: When collecting information, I said in my introductory statement, I said that I collected data and also did reconnaissance. So we had to know where the confrontation lines were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Tell me if I'm correct, Brigadier, but not only do you have to know where the enemy is, but you also have to know where your own forces are, so you can avoid some vulnerable part of the line being taken by surprise; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: No. I just needed to know the lines of confrontation when applying this method of gathering information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, when you gathered the information, Brigadier, you would do it, also, through means of reconnaissance?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you explain in greater detail what you mean by "reconnaissance"?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: The notion of reconnaissance means collecting data by sending units to the other side, to the enemy side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you have any difficulty in sending units to the other side to collect that data?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you send those -- were the units that you sent behind enemy lines specially trained units, specially trained soldiers who had been trained in the area of avoiding detection, how to, essentially, reconnoitre and remain concealed behind enemy lines?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: They weren't trained soldiers. These were mostly locals from those villages or soldiers who had been on that territory and had been driven out so that they were familiar with the routes, the communications, what the enemy had under its control, and what it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you use specially trained soldiers of the HVO to penetrate Serb lines?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: I didn't understand the word "penetrate."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: By the word "penetrate," Brigadier, I mean to go behind enemy lines?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: I said that mostly these were soldiers -- actually, we didn't have time for the training of soldiers, so those of us who were a little braver, we explained to them what kind of data they needed to collect, and passages were discovered, concealed ways, and we trained them as we went along. We didn't have specially trained troops to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you about your headquarters that you had. You were initially -- your initial intelligence headquarters was located at the Hotel Vitez; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you transfer to the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where did you leave after you transferred. I'm sorry. Where did you go after you left the municipal headquarters of the HVO in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: We went to Command B which, at that time, was in Kruscica, and after that I received a task by the commander to arrange and organise my own office at Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I see. Then I misunderstood your testimony. Thank you for correcting me. When did you leave Kruscica and go to Nova Bila?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Not at Kruscica. My office was not at Kruscica. I would go to Kruscica if there was a need for it, but I was in an office in Nova Bila. It was in the forestry building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just so I understand your testimony, Brigadier, you were in the municipal headquarters of the Territorial Defence in Novi Travnik. Then did you transfer to a forestry building in Novi Travnik or in Nova Bila?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please just take me through the series of locations that you went after you were in the municipal headquarters in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: What I said was, after I was at the Municipal Staff at Novi Travnik, I became the head of the Intelligence Services in the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia which, at that time, was at Kruscica, which is in the municipality of Vitez and was in a motel, but my office, my department, was at Nova Bila. As I said, it was in the building of the forestry. There were offices there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, that office of yours, Brigadier, remained there throughout the remainder of the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did Colonel Blaskic have an intelligence liaison officer in his main headquarters in 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: I was the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How did you transmit your intelligence reports to Colonel Blaskic who was located some distance from Nova Bila?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: By courier, while it was possible, and later on, we used modem and fax, a telephone fax.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have Exhibit 173 placed on the -- I'm sorry, Mr. Usher. Could I have Exhibit 172 placed on the easel?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Brigadier, you may be able to help me on this or you may not be able to. Exhibit 172 is an aerial image that, I believe, takes in part of Nova Bila. If you could see and locate your headquarters on that aerial, if it's visible at all, I would ask you to please point it out. Brigadier, the image may not go down far enough south, and your headquarters may not be on that image, but if it is, would you take a look and help us out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Maybe you can leave some space for the Judges as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Brigadier, perhaps I can assist you. I may be able to assist you, Brigadier, if I can orient you on this.

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm pointing to the BRITBAT base. This is Stari Bila. The top of the photograph is in the direction of Vitez --

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- and this is in the direction of Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: If this is Nova Bila, then these two buildings here or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is the direction of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, what was the question that you've asked there because --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I asked the witness if he could identify his headquarters location of Nova Bila on this particular photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Brigadier, could you answer this question in the most precise way you can? I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't see Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Nova Bila is on the map, perhaps counsel can assist him. That appears to be the stumbling point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I indicated to the witness that his headquarters may not appear on that photograph. Apparently, it does not, and I'm prepared to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Proceed then, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, approximately how many kilometres away from the Hotel Vitez was your intelligence headquarters in Nova Bila?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Some five to six kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On the main route between Nova Bila and the Hotel Vitez near the BRITBAT base, there was a prominent hill feature at Grbavica that was maintained and occupied by soldiers from the Armija; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: As I understood the testimony earlier, that feature resulted in the main road between Vitez and Nova Bila being a dangerous route for HVO personnel to travel upon?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is it not correct, Brigadier, that a commander needs intelligence information and good intelligence information at his disposal in every circumstance?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: I don't understand. What do you mean "under every circumstance"?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is it important for a military commander to have at his disposal, and at his immediate disposal, intelligence information that relates to the location and movements of the enemy?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You were a number of kilometres away from his headquarters and in a position where the Muslims could interdict the road between your headquarters and the Hotel Vitez; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did that present any problems for you in terms of relaying information, intelligence information, to Colonel Blaskic in the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: No. I used other means, not only by messenger. There were other means too. As I've said, I forwarded the information by telephone, by telephone modem, or by fax.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were these telephone modems or fax machines reliable?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Mostly, yes. The modem was reliable, while faxes could have been intercepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The modem, did it have the ability to encrypt messages that were sent from Nova Bila to the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How about the fax? Did the fax have the ability to encrypt messages from your headquarters to the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there any point in time in 1993 when the modem that could send encrypted messages from your headquarters to the Hotel Vitez did not work?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: There might have been circumstances where it did not work, but I couldn't give you an exact answer to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I take it if it did not work, it was put back in working order in a very short period of time because that would be critical to any military commander having access to coded information; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes, bearing in mind the possibilities at the time, whether we could repair it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How big of a staff did you have at your headquarters in Nova Bila?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: It was not really a command. It was a department. We did not command at all. Our department had eight people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were those eight people intelligence officers or did that include clerical staff as well?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes. That was also clerical staff, and there were two people who were intelligence officers, another two.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who were they?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: How do you mean, who were they? You mean the other ones or these other two or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What were their names, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: One was Zvonko Bajo, and the other one was Stefan Dujimacic (phoen).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, how often would you send reports, intelligence reports, from your headquarters in Nova Bila, from April of 1993 to the end of the war, to General Blaskic's headquarters in the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Daily. We were sending out reports every day, and the estimates would be sent depending on the needs and depending on the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where, in the Hotel Vitez, would General Blaskic receive those reports? In his office? In a different part of the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: I think that the reports were arriving in the operational centre. The operational department received it and then forwarded it to General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you tell us where the operational centre was?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: I didn't mean the operational centre. I mean the operatives. That's a different thing. The operatives is what I call the people who were on duty, and they were collecting reports that would arrive from the theatre, and then they would see how important they were and would inform the commander about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My question, Brigadier, is very simple: Where, in the Hotel Vitez, would the reports from the theatre be received?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: How can I explain? It was on the ground floor near the entrance on one side. To the right of the corridor was the office of General Blaskic, and on the left-hand side, that means just opposite, were the operatives who received these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were they located in a particular room near Colonel Blaskic where they received these reports? Was there a room that was devoted to the receipt of communications?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Just on the other side of the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What kind of equipment did that room have in it?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: They had modem equipment and fax. The same things that I had to send it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: (Question inaudible - answer being translated simultaneously)

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You were the head of intelligence. You didn't know whether there were any radio equipment receivers in the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That wasn't the question, Mr. President. The prior question was whether there were radios where the duty officer sat in a particular room, and counsel is now turning that on its head, and we object. If he wants to ask the witness whether there were any radios in the Hotel Vitez, period, that's a different question, and he can ask that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What is the question that you are going to ask with reference to the objection just made by Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Brigadier, did the Hotel Vitez have radio receivers in it in 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know what packet communications are, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: I know the modem ones because I saw them. They existed in my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Have you heard of the term "packet communications"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Maybe I should ask the interpreters. Is it what is called in French "communications par paquets"? What is it? What was your question, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My question was, is he familiar with the term "packet communications," and could he explain what they are?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, I'm very happy you don't ask me that question because I'm very impatient. I would like to know the answer. What are packet communications?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, packet communications, at least what I saw, if that is what you mean, is to establish a connection with a radio receiver, and a computer that writes out the messages and sends them out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the Hotel Vitez, in 1993, have a packet communications system?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: I think it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you were also familiar, Brigadier, were you not, with your subordinate -- did you have subordinates in the brigades who were intelligence commanders?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: No. There were not commanders for intelligence duties. It was the deputies or the assistants. They did not have a commanding function.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I see. Did they report to you in the chain of command or did they report to somebody else?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: They reported directly to the commander, but professionally, they would also forward their reports from their units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you about the reconnaissance function of intelligence gathering. When you sent a reconnaissance team out into the field, how did they report back to you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: These were mostly people from units, mostly five to six people, and they would have a direct link with my deputies, those people who were in the units, what we've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say "direct link," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: What I wanted to say was that we could not have the role of commanding, any commanding role. That was up to the unit. In the HVO, everything was organised according to units. The Operative Zone of Central Bosnia did not have its reconnaissance unit which would be subordinate to the commander of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would your reconnaissance teams that went behind enemy territory use any form of communication to communicate back directly to HVO units within the pocket? Did they use radios, hand-held radios? Did they have other means of communication back to the intelligence operatives inside the pocket?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: They should have had it, but at that time, we did not dispose of any such equipment, but the equipment like hand-held radios are very easy to detect. In that case, the mission would probably be jeopardised. So those units would go out in the field and then come back and report after that. It was very rare that we sent out reports from the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you, in addition to receiving intelligence information from the methods you've described, receive intelligence information from the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you receive any intelligence information from Croatian army soldiers who were in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: I do not know of them being in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You do not know of any Croatian soldiers being in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: No. Personally, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, will we be going beyond 6.00 or will we conclude at 6.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Normally, we would end, because this would be the end of our afternoon session, but maybe you have finished by now. How much time do you need still?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have some additional questions, Mr. President. I'll need at least another hour and a half or two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. In that case, I think that we can stop now, and we'll start again tomorrow at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 5.59 p.m. to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 22nd day of September, 1998 at 10.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
